top_story_title: Barracuda chained pre-auth bypass and command injection give root on affected appliances
top_story_summary: Barracuda has disclosed two vulnerabilities in its products that can be chained by an attacker: a pre-authentication authorization bypass and a command injection flaw. Chained, they give command execution with root privileges on a susceptible device. One of the two has been assigned CVE-2026-116606 with a CVSS score of 9.3; the second CVE identifier is not stated in the available reporting. Barracuda has warned customers directly to patch.
top_actions: Inventory every Barracuda appliance you operate (model, firmware/build, management exposure) and check each against the fixed release named in Barracuda's own advisory - no version number has been published in secondary reporting, so take it from the vendor.
Apply the vendor fix, or the documented workaround if no maintenance window is available yet; in HA or clustered deployments upgrade the secondary first and verify config sync afterwards.
Remove the appliance management and administrative interfaces from the public internet immediately; restrict them to a dedicated management VLAN or out-of-band network with an ACL.
Treat a pre-auth root path as a possible prior compromise: after patching, rotate local admin credentials, API tokens, device certificates and any secrets stored on the appliance.

Export and review the appliance configuration for unexpected admin accounts, scripts, forwarding rules or modified web resources, and check for processes or cron entries running as root that you did not create.
executive_summary: Barracuda disclosed two chainable vulnerabilities - a pre-authentication authorization bypass and a command injection - that together give root on affected appliances; CVE-2026-116606 carries CVSS 9.3.
No confirmed exploitation and no KEV listing yet, and EPSS for CVE-2026-116606 is low (0.007); the pre-auth nature means that can change fast.
No fixed release or affected product list appears in the reporting - get both from the Barracuda advisory for each model you run, and do not act on a version number from a news article.

Nothing else in this window concerned network infrastructure: the one other item, Google's takedown of the X.CPE botnet, was Android TV set-top boxes and Android IoT, not routers, switches or gateways.
key_actions: **Barracuda** — Identify affected devices from your asset inventory filtered by Barracuda model and running firmware version.

**Barracuda** — Confirm the running version against Barracuda's fixed-release table and schedule the upgrade in the change window; in an HA pair upgrade the secondary first, then fail over and upgrade the primary.
**Barracuda** — Treat this as the same remediation track as the lead item - do not open a second change record.
**Barracuda** — Pull the advisory from Barracuda's own security notification channel to get the affected product list and fixed builds, since the press coverage states neither.
